# Group Reflection

## Skills inventory

### Functions & refactoring (W2)

**What we did:**

We wrote a custom function called `hour_midpoint()` to convert interval-coded
time responses such as `"2-4"` and `"4-6"` into approximate numeric midpoint
values. We used the resulting variables for the permutation test and logistic
regression.

We also moved shared package loading and data preparation into `setup.R`, so
that several Quarto pages could use the same cleaned dataset without repeating
all code.

**What worked well:**

The helper function reduced repeated `case_when()` code and made the conversion
process consistent. Using `setup.R` also improved consistency across the
different `.qmd` files.

**What was hard:**

The raw data contained several different interval formats, so it was easy to
miss categories. For example, values such as `"3-4"` had to be added after
checking the raw responses. We also had to keep variable names consistent
between `Dataset.qmd`, `InitialDataAnalysis.qmd`, and
`ConfirmatoryDataAnalysis.qmd`.

### Debugging (W3)

**What we did:**

We debugged R errors, Quarto rendering problems, incorrect factor levels,
missing package calls, and Git synchronization issues. We used functions such
as `glimpse()`, `summary()`, `count()`, `unique()`, and missing-value checks to
inspect the data and identify problems.

**What worked well:**

Testing small sections separately helped us locate errors. Looking at the raw
values before recoding was especially useful because some apparent missing
values were actually unmatched category labels.

**What was hard:**

Git problems were harder than most R errors. We encountered merge conflicts,
rebasing issues, a detached `HEAD`, and non-fast-forward push errors. These
situations were difficult because the correct command depended on the current
repository state.

### Version control & remotes (W4)

**What we did:**

We used Git and GitHub to share files, record changes, and synchronize the
project repository. Group members committed their work and pulled or pushed
changes to the shared remote.

**What worked well:**

GitHub gave us a visible history of the project and allowed us to work on
different parts of the analysis.

**What was hard:**

Our original workflow proposal described feature branches and pull requests,
but in practice we often worked directly on `main`. This was simpler, but it
also caused merge conflicts when more than one person edited the same file.
We also learned that committing before pulling can create unnecessary
divergence. 

It was tried to limit direct pushes to main branch trough the repository configurations, but somehow someone (that was not the repo creater) could always push without pull requests.

### Quarto websites & collaborative coding (W5)

**What we did:**

We organised the project as a Quarto website with separate pages for the
dataset, initial data analysis, confirmatory analysis, workflow organisation,
and group reflection.

**What worked well:**

Quarto allowed us to combine prose, code, tables, statistical output, and
visualisations in reproducible pages. Code folding and the table of contents
made the pages easier to navigate.

**What was hard:**

At one point, the same material appeared in both the proposal and the split analysis files. This created duplication and raised the risk that the files would become inconsistent over time. We also had to spend extra effort fixing YAML formatting and ensuring that page titles and variable names matched across all documents.

Even after eliminating the duplicates, rendering the Quarto website proved to be extremely time-consuming. We encountered numerous unexpected YAML errors and file path issues, which led to significant troubleshooting and cost us a lot of time just trying to get the site to render successfully.

### R packages (W6)

**What we did:**

We used:

- `tidyverse` for data import, cleaning, transformation, and plotting;
- `infer` for the permutation test;
- `ggplot2` for static visualisation;
- `patchwork` for combining plots;
- `plotly` for an interactive family-time visualisation;
- `broom` for tidying model output;
- `gt` for the logistic regression table;
- `knitr` for rendered tables;
- `scales` for percentage labels;
- `renv` for recording package versions.

**What worked well:**

The packages worked together well and supported a complete workflow from raw
data to a rendered website.

**What was hard:**

We occasionally used packages in a page without loading them in the shared
setup. We also had to remove duplicate library calls and ensure that every
group member had compatible package versions.

### Initial data analysis & data cleaning (W7)

**What we did:**

We renamed the long survey questions to shorter variable names, recoded one
incorrect `profession = "male"` entry to `NA`, converted interval-coded time
variables into numeric midpoints, and created a binary addiction variable.

We explored the data with summaries, frequency tables, missing-value checks,
and visualisations of age, screen time, family time, advertising influence,
and self-reported addiction.

**What worked well:**

The data cleaning was documented clearly, and the exploratory plots helped us
understand the sample before fitting models. We discovered that the sample was
strongly concentrated among young respondents and students.

**What was hard:**

The dataset had no detailed codebook, so we had to infer the meaning of some
response categories. The time variables were recorded as broad intervals
rather than exact values. Converting these intervals to midpoints introduced
approximation error.

The `"not sure"` addiction group was also substantial. Excluding it from the
binary regression reduced the effective sample size.

### Reproducibility, open data & renv (W9)

**What we did:**

We used a publicly available dataset from Mendeley Data under a CC BY 4.0
licence. We committed `renv.lock` and the required `renv` files to the
repository.

We also excluded the respondent name variable from all analysis because it was
not needed and could potentially identify individuals.

**What worked well:**

The data source, licence, cleaning steps, and package environment were
documented, making the project more transparent and reproducible.

**What was hard:**

The dataset itself was publicly available, but it did not include a full
codebook or detailed sampling documentation. Therefore, reproducibility of our
code was stronger than the representativeness of the underlying survey.

### Analysis & inference strategies (W10)

**What we did:**

We initially considered five research questions, but after receiving feedback
we narrowed the project to two:

1. Is social media time associated with time spent with family?
2. Can self-reported social media addiction be predicted from social media
   hours, forgetting about time, age, and gender?

For the first question, we used a permutation test for the slope between
numeric midpoint versions of social media time and family time.

For the second question, we fitted a multiple logistic regression model with
`addicted_bin` as the binary outcome.

**What worked well:**

Reducing the number of questions allowed us to complete the analyses rather
than leaving several questions at the planning stage. The selected methods
matched the final variable structures more closely than our earlier ideas.

**What was hard:**

For the family-time question, both variables were originally ordinal interval
categories. We had to decide whether treating midpoint values as numeric was
defensible. We chose to proceed while clearly acknowledging the approximation.

Interpreting the logistic regression also required care. We had to distinguish
between odds and probabilities and avoid making causal claims from
observational survey data.

### Communication & visualisation (W11)

**What we did:**

We created proportion bar charts, histograms, grouped bar charts, a stacked
interactive Plotly chart, and a formatted `gt` table for the logistic
regression results.

**What worked well:**

The visualisations made the main patterns easier to communicate. The `gt`
table was especially useful because it presented odds ratios, confidence
intervals, and p-values in a readable format.

**What was hard:**

Some early interpretations were too strong. For example, we initially used
phrases such as “tipping point” or implied that screen time directly reduced
family time. We later changed the wording to describe associations and sample
patterns more cautiously.

We also discovered that manually setting incorrect factor levels could
silently remove observations from plots.

## Key analytical decisions

### Decision 1: Continue with the original dataset

**What were we deciding between?**

We considered whether to switch to another dataset because our survey data had
a student-heavy sample, interval-coded variables, inconsistent entries, and no
complete codebook.

**How did we reason through it?**

By the time we considered changing datasets, we had already cleaned the data,
written the helper function, produced exploratory plots, and developed the
analysis plan. Starting again would have reduced the time available for
completing the statistical analyses.

We decided that the dataset was still suitable for demonstrating the course
workflow, provided that we described its limitations honestly.

**In hindsight, would we decide differently?**

Probably not. The dataset was imperfect, but those imperfections gave us
useful experience with data cleaning, missing values, recoding, and cautious
interpretation. For a future project, we would examine the documentation and
sampling design more carefully before committing to a dataset.

### Decision 2: Reduce five research questions to two

**What were we deciding between?**

Our early proposal contained five research questions. We had to choose between
covering all five superficially or completing a smaller number in more depth.

**How did we reason through it?**

The feedback recommended committing to the two focus questions. We kept the
family-time association question and the addiction prediction question because
they used different analytical approaches and were already connected to our
cleaned variables.

**In hindsight, would we decide differently?**

No. The final project became more coherent after reducing the scope. We were
able to include both visual exploration and inferential analysis for the
selected questions.

### Decision 3: Convert hour intervals to numeric midpoints

**What were we deciding between?**

We considered keeping the hour variables as ordered categories or converting
them to approximate numeric values.

**How did we reason through it?**

The permutation slope test and logistic regression required numeric predictors.
Using midpoints provided a practical approximation while preserving the order
and approximate scale of the categories.

**In hindsight, would we decide differently?**

We would still use the midpoint conversion, but we would document it earlier
and verify all raw response categories before producing any plots or models. We
would also consider sensitivity analyses using the original ordered categories.

## Workflow & collaboration

**How did we divide work across group members?**

Group members worked on different parts of the repository, including the
dataset documentation, exploratory visualisations, confirmatory analysis,
workflow description, and final website text. Shared tasks included data
cleaning, reviewing code, and fixing rendering or Git problems.

**What branching or Git workflow did we actually use, and did it match the
proposal?**

Our proposal described a feature-branch workflow with pull requests and
automated checks. In practice, we mostly worked directly on the shared `main`
branch and used regular commits, pulls, and pushes.

Therefore, the actual workflow did not fully match the proposal. We also did
not implement the planned pre-commit linting process consistently.

**What worked well in our coordination?**

Dividing the project into separate `.qmd` pages made it possible for different
members to contribute independently. GitHub commit history also made it
possible to track progress and recover earlier versions.

**What was harder than expected?**

Coordination became difficult when multiple people edited the same file or
when local repositories were not synchronized before new commits. Merge
conflicts and inconsistent copies of duplicated content cost time.

**What would we change?**

We would assign one owner to each file, pull before starting work, use feature
branches for substantial edits, and avoid keeping the same content in multiple
documents.

## LLM usage

### Usage 1: Data cleaning and helper functions

- **Tool / model:** ChatGPT
- **What it produced:** Suggested renaming code, missing-value checks, and the
  structure of the `hour_midpoint()` function.
- **What we had to correct or verify:** We checked the actual raw category
  values and added missing mappings such as `"3-4"`. We also verified that
  recoding `"not sure"` as `NA` was appropriate only for the binary model.

### Usage 2: Selecting statistical methods

- **Tool / model:** ChatGPT
- **What it produced:** Suggestions including t-tests, correlations,
  permutation tests, chi-square tests, and logistic regression.
- **What we had to correct or verify:** A two-sample t-test was not suitable
  because the explanatory variable was not binary. We replaced it with a
  permutation test for linear association. We also checked that the logistic
  regression formula matched the variables actually used in the project.

### Usage 3: Interpretation of results

- **Tool / model:** ChatGPT
- **What it produced:** Draft explanations of plots, p-values, confidence
  intervals, odds ratios, and model findings.
- **What we had to correct or verify:** Some generated wording was too causal
  or too confident. We replaced terms such as “tipping point,” “dependency,”
  and “directly reduces” with more cautious descriptions of associations in
  this sample.

### Usage 4: Git troubleshooting

- **Tool / model:** ChatGPT
- **What it produced:** Suggested commands for resolving merge conflicts,
  rebases, detached `HEAD` states, and rejected pushes.
- **What we had to correct or verify:** Git advice had to be checked against
  `git status` because a command that is correct in one repository state may be
  harmful in another. In one case, we decided to abandon local changes and
  reset the repository to `origin/main`.

### Usage 5: Quarto structure and writing

- **Tool / model:** ChatGPT
- **What it produced:** Draft page structures, YAML suggestions, headings,
  reflection text, and revisions to the analysis descriptions.
- **What we had to correct or verify:** We changed generic text so that it
  reflected our actual workflow. We also corrected mismatched variable names,
  duplicated packages, broken YAML, and claims about tools such as feature
  branches or pre-commit hooks that we had planned but not fully used.
  
### Usage 6: Quarto webpage refinement and Git conflict resolution

- **Tool / model:** Gemini (Google)
- **What it produced:** Precise corrections for webpage rendering failures,
  remediation of broken Quarto/Markdown syntax, and line-by-line resolutions
  for complex Git merge conflicts (particularly within `.gitignore` and
  `InitialDataAnalysis.qmd`).
- **What we had to correct or verify:** We manually verified each conflict
  resolution in RStudio to ensure that no group member's analytical code or
  updated package requirements were accidentally overwritten during the branch
  integration process.

## One LLM error or mistake we caught

One important mistake was a recommendation to use a two-sample t-test for a
question where the explanatory variable contained more than two categories.
The assumptions of that method did not match the data structure. After
reviewing the variables, we instead used a permutation test based on the slope
between family time and social media time.

We also caught several smaller issues, including suggested variable names that
did not match the cleaned dataset and interpretations that overstated what the
plots could demonstrate.

## What surprised us

We expected higher social media use to show a clear negative relationship with
family time. However, the permutation test did not provide evidence of a
statistically significant linear association in this sample.

We were also surprised by how strongly the dataset was dominated by students
and young adults. This made us more cautious about generalising the findings to
the wider population.

## What our analysis cannot answer

The project cannot establish that social media use causes addiction or reduces
family time. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, and respondents
were not randomly assigned to different levels of social media use.

The analysis also cannot represent the general population reliably because the
sample is heavily concentrated among students. In addition, the use of broad
hour intervals limits precision.

## Skill development

One concept that became clearer through the project was the difference between
exploratory patterns and confirmatory evidence. A graph can suggest a trend,
but a statistical test or model is needed to assess uncertainty, and even a
statistically significant association does not establish causality.

Git also became more understandable through practical use. Concepts such as
remotes, branches, conflicts, rebasing, and detached `HEAD` states were much
clearer after we encountered them in the shared repository.

## What we would learn next

A useful next step would be learning how to evaluate logistic regression more
fully, including model diagnostics, predicted probabilities, calibration, and
out-of-sample validation.

We would also like to learn methods that handle ordinal interval-coded
variables without converting them into approximate midpoints, as well as more
structured collaborative Git workflows using feature branches and pull
requests.
